overview: This record concerns Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian administration, rather than an independent kingdom. Occupation began in 1878 while the Ottoman sultan formally retained sovereignty; annexation followed in 1908. Railways, museums and new institutions developed amid unequal imperial power and diverse local communities.

periods.title: Occupation and administration
periods.summary: Austria-Hungary administered the territory while Ottoman sovereignty formally remained.

periods.title: Annexation and limited representation
periods.summary: Annexation was followed by a constitutional statute and Council, but major authority remained with the imperial administration.

items.text: The 1910 statute introduced a representative Council, but supreme administration remained with the Joint Ministry of Finance in Vienna. Having an assembly did not mean that residents controlled all the decisions affecting their lives.

Zemaljski ustav (statut) za Bosnu i Hercegovinu means “Provincial constitution (statute) for Bosnia and Herzegovina.” The Parliament’s monograph reproduces this 1910 document title. It is a contemporary South Slavic text in Latin letters, alongside a German version.

The Council’s work was interrupted during the First World War, and the emperor abolished it in 1915. This falls just beyond the atlas’s 1914 endpoint. The history of representation did not progress smoothly in one direction.

Railway construction began soon after the 1878 occupation. The early narrow-gauge system used equipment transferred from an earlier construction project. Builders adapted what they could obtain rather than beginning with a perfectly standardized railway.

Early passenger accommodation could be improvised from freight vehicles, with cloth roofs and curtains added. Travelling by train did not automatically mean a comfortable carriage. Transport history includes the experience of sitting through the journey as well as laying track.

The museum library began operating in 1888. At first, curators managed it alongside their other duties; Franjo Topič later became its specialist librarian. Sorting and preserving information was a practical part of building a research institution.

The library moved into new museum buildings in 1913. Its collections brought together archaeology, history, plants, animals and geology. Researchers could compare objects and written studies across subjects rather than treating the past as only a list of rulers.

sections.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book

items.text: The Despić house belonged to a wealthy Orthodox merchant family. Its oldest part dates to the 1600s and later additions altered it. The building preserves a layered household history, not a house created all at once in 1878.

The Despić brothers staged plays to entertain their guests. A domestic gathering could become a small theatre. This is an example from a prosperous urban household, not evidence that every family had a stage in the sitting room.

Makso Despić served as a treasurer under Ottoman rule and later as a city councillor under Austria-Hungary. One person’s career crossed an imperial transition, showing how local experience could continue while the government above it changed.

In 1894 the National Museum purchased the Sarajevo Haggadah from the local Sephardic Koen family. The manuscript was made much earlier outside Bosnia. Its acquisition records a specific Sarajevo family connection, rather than a medieval Bosnian place of manufacture.

A haggadah organizes the readings and rituals of the Passover Seder, a family meal with guests. This copy combines Hebrew writing, parchment leaves and painted scenes. Its purpose connects sophisticated bookmaking with people reading and listening around a table.

ending.text: Austro-Hungarian rule ended in 1918 as the monarchy disintegrated. Authority passed through a local National Council and Bosnia and Herzegovina entered the new South Slav kingdom. The atlas’s 1914 endpoint therefore stops before the administrative period ended; its communities and institutions had further, changing histories.
